property_summary: For every caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(x) sets the public owner storage to exactly the provided address x (i.e., c.owner() == x); the mutant which casts to payable on assignment can make c.owner() differ from x for some inputs (fuzzer will find an address where the stored owner != supplied address).

For any caller who is the current owner and any address candidate, calling setOwner(candidate) results in c.owner() equaling the supplied candidate (the reference assigns the raw address while the mutant's payable(...) cast can change the stored representation and thus break equality for some candidate addresses).

For every address candidate a and when called by the current owner, C.setOwner(a) leaves c.owner() equal to the canonical non-payable address value of a (i.e. storing the raw address) — the mutant that assigns owner = payable(a) can store a different value for some addresses that are contracts with non-zero codehash/payable-ness (the cast may interact with type expectations and change stored value in mutated AST), so there exists some fuzzed address input that makes c.owner() != a on the mutant but always c.owner() == a on the reference.

For every caller that is the current owner and for every address candidate a (possibly a contract), invoking setOwner(a) on the correct contract stores exactly the 20-byte non-payable address value such that c.owner() == a (i.e. the returned getter equals the supplied address); the mutant that introduces owner = payable(_owner) can produce a different stored value when _owner is a contract address with code (so there exists some fuzzed contract address input that makes the mutant's c.owner() != a while the reference always preserves equality).

For every address caller (the current owner) and any target address a, after setOwner(a) returns successfully the public owner getter returns an address whose non-payable conversion equals a (i.e., address(uint160(c.owner())) == a); the mutant with a payable-cast can produce a stored owner whose cast-back-to-address differs for some inputs, so this rule is violated by the mutant.

For any caller who is the current owner and calls setOwner(x), the contract's owner becomes exactly the provided argument x; the mutant that uses tx.origin instead can change owner to a different address (tx.origin) and thus will violate this when msg.sender != tx.origin (e.g., when owner calls through a contract).

For any caller who is the current owner and calls setOwner(addr), the contract's owner becomes the provided addr; the mutant that assigns tx.origin instead will break this when the owner calls via an intermediate contract (msg.sender != tx.origin) so owner != provided addr.

If the current owner calls setOwner(newOwner) then after the call C.owner() equals the provided newOwner for every admissible input; the mutant that assigns tx.origin breaks this when the owner calls setOwner through an intermediate contract (so msg.sender != tx.origin) because owner becomes tx.origin instead of the supplied argument.

For any caller who is the current owner and calls setOwner(newOwner) directly (msg.sender == tx.origin), the contract's owner becomes the supplied newOwner; the mutant that uses tx.origin instead only preserves this when msg.sender == tx.origin, so the difference is revealed when the owner calls setOwner through an intermediate contract (msg.sender != tx.origin) — the reference still sets owner to the supplied newOwner but the mutant sets it to tx.origin.

If the current owner calls setOwner(viaContract, newOwner) through an intermediate caller contract, the reference sets owner to the supplied newOwner (owner == newOwner) for all such calls, while the mutant that uses tx.origin will instead set owner to the tx.origin (breaking the equality) for some intermediate-caller inputs.

For any caller address A and any target address T, when A calls setOwner(T) on the correct contract, the owner becomes T only if A was the current owner (i.e., onlyOwner checks msg.sender); the mutant that uses tx.origin can be bypassed by making a call through a contract (so an intermediate contract can change owner even if the immediate caller isn't the owner), violating this rule for some inputs.

For all callers A and newOwner N, when A (the direct msg.sender) calls setOwner(N) on the reference contract, the owner becomes N iff A was the prior owner (onlyOwner uses msg.sender); the mutant that checks tx.origin allows a call routed through an intermediate contract to change owner even when the intermediate contract is the msg.sender but tx.origin is the original owner, thus breaking that ownership-check invariant for some inputs.

Invariant: only the current owner (msg.sender == owner) can successfully call setOwner and change the stored owner; the mutant removes this check allowing non-owners to change owner, violating the invariant for some caller input.
General rule: only the deploying owner can change C.owner via setOwner (for any caller address); the mutant removing the require allows some caller address to change owner, violating this rule.

General rule: after any caller who is the current owner calls setOwner(newOwner), the contract's owner becomes newOwner; the mutant requiring msg.sender == address(0) prevents any real owner call from succeeding (reverts) so the owner does not change for such inputs.

For any caller address X, when X is the current owner and calls setOwner(Y), the call succeeds and c.owner() == Y afterwards; the mutant that requires msg.sender == address(0) causes such owner calls from real addresses to revert (so the property is violated for some fuzzed owner/caller addresses).

For any caller addr and any newOwner addr, if the caller is the current owner then calling setOwner(newOwner) succeeds and c.owner() equals newOwner afterwards; the mutant that requires msg.sender == address(0) causes real-owner calls to revert, breaking this property for some fuzzed owner/caller addresses.

For any address caller and any address newOwner, if caller is the contract's current owner then calling setOwner(newOwner) returns true (succeeds) and afterwards c.owner() == newOwner; the mutant that only allows msg.sender == address(0) causes such a legitimate owner call to revert (fail) for some fuzzed owner/caller, breaking the rule.
